Forecast calibration

How good is the Luxembourg weather forecast?

When a forecast says "40% chance of rain", does it rain on 40% of those days? Checked against real station measurements across 15 European capitals.

The short answer for Luxembourg

The Luxembourg rain forecast is moderately skilful, though 4 points on its probability scale are off by more than chance explains.

When it says rain is near certain (99%), believe about 76%. When it says rain is very unlikely (1%), there is still roughly a 9% chance.

Based on 727 days, 2024-04-26 to 2026-05-01. "Rain" means at least 0.2 mm measured at LUXEMBOURG AIRPORT, 5.4 km from the forecast grid point. Skill score 0.26, ranked 10 of 15 — but see the rank range (6–14) before reading anything into that position.

Is Bucharest unusual? The other European capitals

One city cannot tell you whether a forecast is good or merely typical. The identical pipeline was therefore run over every European capital with a usable rain gauge. Of 43 capitals probed, 18 had a station close enough and current enough, and 15 survived the data checks once the records arrived.

Bucharest ranks 5 of 15 (skill 0.41), but the honest statement is the rank range: 3–8. With about two years per city, most of the ordering is not resolvable, and a league table with a winner would be reading noise. The rank column is deliberately a range for every city.
The same bias appears in every capital. Low-probability days rain more often than stated in 15 of 15 capitals with a confidence interval excluding zero, and high-probability days rain less often than stated in 14 of 15. So the reversal of the published consumer "wet bias" is not a Bucharest quirk — it is what this forecast chain does everywhere, and it is the strongest evidence here that we are looking at raw model output rather than a hand-tuned product. Bucharest happens to be one of the mildest cases at the low end (+1.9%); the most extreme is Reykjavik at +48.6%.

What explains the spread?

Almost entirely how often it rains. Skill falls as the base rate rises (correlation -0.77, permutation p = 0.001): the wet Atlantic capitals are genuinely harder, not badly served. Distance from the gauge to the forecast grid point explains nothing at all (-0.01, p = 0.97), which is reassuring — it means the ranking is not an artefact of which cities happen to have a close station.

This cuts against the intuition behind ForecastWatch's "maritime locations are more predictable" framing. On a categorical accuracy rate, a dry climate scores well by saying "dry"; on a skill score, which removes that advantage, the maritime capitals come out worse, and Reykjavik — where it rains 77% of days — cannot beat its own climatology at all.

And temperature, for scale

The same capitals, on daily-max temperature error against lead time. The median capital sits at 1.03 °C one day ahead and 2.14 °C seven days ahead, once each site's constant offset is removed. meteoblue publish 1.66 °C for the best raw model at day one globally, so this archive is in the expected place — a reassurance that nothing in the pipeline is quietly broken.

Whose forecast is this, actually?

A league table only means something if every row is the same forecaster. It was not. Open-Meteo's default best_match picks a model per location, and across these capitals it resolves to ICON-EU in 7 of them and ECMWF IFS in 8. That identification is not inferred from a correlation: across three widely separated months the default series matches the pinned model's value in every single hour. Probability of precipitation is strongly model-dependent — at Bucharest, over identical days, ICON scores 0.41 and ECMWF 0.30 — so this had every opportunity to be the real reason one city outranked another.

The entire table was therefore rebuilt twice, pinning one model everywhere:

The ranking survives. Bucharest sits at 6 of 15 with ICON pinned everywhere and 6 of 15 with ECMWF pinned, against 5 as published. The gap between the ICON-served and ECMWF-served groups is +0.19 skill as published and +0.19 with the model held fixed — essentially unchanged. Model and geography were confounded, but the geography is what does the work: best_match sends ECMWF to the wet Atlantic capitals, and those really are harder.

The exercise paid for itself in a different way. ICON's advantage is not uniform — it tracks how often it rains (r = −0.64, p = 0.010). The high-resolution regional model wins where rain is infrequent and largely convective (Vienna +0.16, Bucharest +0.10), and loses where fronts arrive off the ocean (Dublin -0.09). Neither model is simply better, which is presumably why the default routes by region at all.

This came out of an audit, not luck. The study pins its model explicitly for temperature, but the probability series was requested without a model parameter and so silently inherited the default. Checking month by month showed the backing model never changed mid-archive, so no published number was built from a spliced series — but nothing except this check was guaranteeing that.

What was thrown away, and why

The exclusions are part of the result. Two capitals were rejected before any data was downloaded because their nearest qualifying gauge sits on a mountain (Andorra la Vella's is at 2451 m, Vaduz's at 2502 m); verifying a valley city against those would measure the lapse rate, not the forecast. The rest failed once their records were inspected:

  • Budapest — peak r=0.55 margin=0.02 - no clean single lag
  • Chisinau — only 102 usable pairs (< 500)
  • Sarajevo — peak r=0.35 margin=0.04 - no clean single lag

The rain-day convention had to be re-derived for every city separately, and it genuinely differs: the station date needs shifting back a day in Bucharest and Reykjavik, forward a day in Amsterdam, Dublin and Luxembourg, and not at all elsewhere. Assuming Bucharest's convention travelled would have produced confident, wrong curves for a third of the map.

Beyond the capitals: 97 cities

Capitals are a biased sample — they are where the good instruments are. Widening to every city with a usable rain gauge tests whether the previous section's conclusions were about weather forecasting or about capitals.

The selection rule is unchanged and mechanical: a gauge within 25 km, within 300 m of the forecast grid point's elevation, reporting through the verification period. 172 cities passed that screen; 97 then survived the per-city rain-day convention scan and the record-quality checks. Cities sharing a gauge are counted once, so these remain independent samples.

Bucharest ranks 28 of 97 with skill 0.41 — rank range 12–54. Its score is unchanged to three decimals from the single-city and capitals runs, which is the regression test for this whole expansion: adding 96 cities did not perturb the original answer.

Which of the 15-city findings survived

ExplainingDriver 15 capitals97 citiesReplication
bsshow often it rains-0.77 (p=0.001)-0.11 (p=0.291)did not hold
bsscontinentality+0.44 (p=0.097)+0.03 (p=0.764)held
bssgauge distance-0.01 (p=0.975)-0.12 (p=0.224)held
reliabilityhow often it rains+0.81 (p=0.000)+0.55 (p=0.000)held
reliabilitycontinentality-0.33 (p=0.232)+0.07 (p=0.506)held
reliabilitygauge distance+0.10 (p=0.735)-0.02 (p=0.804)held

The honest headline of this section is a failure to replicate. Across 15 capitals, skill looked as though it were largely dictated by how often it rains (r = −0.77, p = 0.001) — a tidy story. At 97 cities that correlation collapses to roughly −0.11 and is no longer distinguishable from chance. It was a small-sample artefact, and had this study stopped at the capitals it would have been reported as a result.

What does survive is the less convenient relationship: calibration error grows with the rain rate (r = +0.56, p < 0.001). Wetter cities are not forecast with less skill, but their stated probabilities sit further from the truth. Gauge distance still explains nothing, which continues to rule out the obvious measurement artefact.

The inversion is not a European quirk either

Low-probability days produce rain more often than stated in 95 of 97 cities (87 with a confidence interval excluding zero), and high-probability days produce rain less often in 93 of 97 (84 significant) — the opposite of the wet bias documented for consumer forecasts in the literature.

The sharper test is the 25 cities outside Europe — Sydney, Montreal, New York, Mexicali and others. They lie outside ICON-EU's domain, so a different model entirely is answering the request. The low-end under-forecasting still appears in 23 of 25 of them (19 significant). Across 15 European capitals this could have been a property of two European models; it now looks like a property of how this kind of forecast is made.

Temperature error vs lead time

The deterministic track over the same cities, as daily-max error after removing each site's constant bias: a median of 1.19 °C at one day ahead, rising to 2.40 °C at seven.

This covers 76 of the 97 cities, not all of them: the deterministic track is the most request-hungry step in the study and runs into the weather API's hourly quota. It stops cleanly and keeps what it has rather than discarding the run, so the figure is a partial but unbiased slice — cities are processed alphabetically, which is unrelated to forecast quality.

The Bucharest deep dive

Everything below this line is Bucharest, whichever city you selected above. These analyses need hourly present-weather reports, a second station for the representativeness floor, and a temperature record long enough to derive frost and heat probabilities. Those exist for Bucharest and not for the other capitals, so the sections are not relabelled to match your selection — that would be inventing results. You currently have Luxembourg selected; its own results are above.

Seasonal calibration curves

I expected summer to be worst, because summer rain here is convective — small, short-lived cells a forecast grid cannot resolve. It is not; spring is. Summer does have the weakest resolution, which is the convective signal, but its low rain rate makes the overall score look better.

Will it rain at 6pm? The hourly check

Everything above asks "will it rain today". That is the easier and less useful question. This section asks whether the forecast is honest hour by hour — and because there are 10,696 hours instead of 731 days, the answer is far better supported.

 Daily Hourly
Sample731 days 10696 hours
Effective sample 3631665
Skill score (higher better) 0.409 0.467
Average error (lower better) 6.5%2.5%
What "almost certain" really means 82% 97%
The confident end is honest after all. On the daily view, "99%" meant 82% — apparent overconfidence. Hour by hour, "98%" means 97%, which is within the range a flawless forecast would give.

Read that carefully — it is not a clean comparison. Three things change at once between the two tracks: the event (at least 0.2 mm accumulated, versus precipitation simply being observed), the station, and the kind of measurement (a rain gauge versus an observer's present-weather report). A brief shower registers as precipitation hour-by-hour while depositing less than 0.2 mm in the gauge. So the most defensible reading is that much of the daily "overconfidence" was an artefact of the rain threshold, not dishonesty in the forecast — consistent with the threshold sensitivity seen in the robustness table.

The low end still misses: hours forecast at 0.5% see precipitation 2.4% of the time, and hours forecast at 13% see it 27% of the time. Both are genuinely outside chance. Low probabilities are understated at every timescale tested.

A caveat found while building this

The three Bucharest stations disagree sharply about how often it rains — and the pattern follows how often each one files a report, not how far it is from the city centre:

StationDistance Reports per hourHours with precipitation
Bucuresti Filaret1.1 km1.05.7%
Baneasa Aurel Vlaicu8.5 km1.310.2%
Henri Coanda / Otopeni16.1 km1.310.5%

The closest station reports the least rain, because it files the fewest reports and so misses brief showers between them. This is observing practice, not weather, and it sets a floor on how precisely any of this can be measured.

Could we just correct it?

If the extremes are overconfident, an obvious fix is to learn a correction. The honest way to measure its value is to train it on some days and test it on different days — otherwise the correction simply memorises the noise and always appears to help.

VersionBrier score Skill score
As published0.1171 0.409
Corrected, tested on unseen days 0.1169 0.410
Result: correcting it gains 0.16%. Essentially nothing. The overconfidence at the extremes is real, but it is small enough — and our record short enough — that a correction learned from 731 days is itself too noisy to help. Both facts matter: the bias exists, and chasing it is not worth it yet.

Does the conclusion survive poking at it?

A result is only worth reporting if it does not depend on arbitrary choices. These runs change the definition of "it rained", and swap the source of truth entirely, then check whether the overconfidence is still there.

What was changed "0%" really means"99%" really means Skill scoreConclusion
threshold 0.1 mm (variant)6%84%0.429held
threshold 0.2 mm (primary)5%82%0.409held
threshold 1.0 mm (variant)2%72%0.258held
truth = ERA5 reanalysis4%98%0.506held
truth = Baneasa station (10km)4%84%0.433held
Held in 5 of 5 variants. The overconfidence at both ends is not an artefact of how rain was defined or which station was used.

Note the ERA5 row: scored against a model-based reconstruction instead of a real gauge, the forecast looks considerably better (skill 0.51). That is the flattery effect of grading a model against another model — and the reason real measurements are used as the primary truth here.

How does this compare with what is already published?

There is no public calibration number for Bucharest — that is the gap this study fills — but there are published accuracy numbers for Europe. ForecastWatch scores 593 European locations on the share of high and low temperature forecasts landing within 3 °F (1.67 °C), and reports a country-level band of roughly 58%–70%. Computing the same quantity here puts the result on a scale someone else has already calibrated.

ForecastLead Temps within 1.67 °C …after removing site bias Day-max error (°C) Rain/no-rain correct
ecmwf_ifs025145%64%1.5982%
icon_eu148%66%1.2683%
persistence144%44%2.6974%
ecmwf_ifs025244%60%1.7280%
icon_eu245%61%1.4679%
persistence233%33%3.8065%
ecmwf_ifs025343%54%1.8177%
icon_eu342%57%1.6179%
persistence328%28%4.2464%

Raw, the day-1 rate is 45% — below the published band. Almost all of that is one fixed offset: the grid point runs +2.5 °C too warm overnight against the Baneasa gauge, while daytime highs are only -0.9 °C off. Subtract that constant and the rate becomes 64%, inside the band. Every provider in the ForecastWatch panel post-processes its output, and removing a site offset is the first thing such post-processing does, so the debiased column is the fairer comparison — though it is fitted on the same days it is scored on, so read it as a ceiling.

Against "tomorrow will be like today". At lead 1 the model beats persistence only narrowly on this tolerance metric (45% vs 44%), because persistence has no site bias to speak of. Its advantage is unmissable elsewhere: day-max error 1.59 °C vs 2.69 °C, rain calls 82% vs 74%, and the gap widens with every extra day of lead.

A hit rate is a weak measure of a probability forecast, which is why it is not the headline here. The rain probabilities score 85% correct when thresholded at 50% — but simply saying "dry" every single day scores 73%, because it only rains on 27% of days. The Brier score above does not have that blind spot.

Does Bucharest show the classic "wet bias"?

The best-known result in this area (Bickel & Kim, 2008) is that a consumer weather provider over-states low rain chances: on days it calls 10%, it rains less often than that. Stating the expectation first turns the curve into a test rather than a story told after the fact.

Days where…Days StatedActually rained Gap (95% CI)
low (PoP <= 20%)475 3.1% 7.4% +4.3% [+2.1%, +7.0%]
high (PoP >= 60%)167 88.0% 76.0% -11.9% [-18.8%, -5.9%]
The opposite happens here. Low-probability days rain more often than stated (+4.3%), and high-probability days rain less often (-11.9%); both intervals exclude zero, and they come from a block bootstrap that respects week-long dry spells rather than pretending consecutive days are independent. That is the signature of raw model output, not of a consumer product: nobody has nudged the low end upward to avoid being blamed for a surprise shower.

Caveat that must travel with these numbers: ForecastWatch uses its own provider panel, station set and quality control, and publishes at country level. A figure landing inside their band is consistent with their measurement, not equal to it. This is positioning, not a ranking.

Frost, heat and rain — and how far ahead each is worth trusting

Everything so far has been about rain, because rain is the only thing the archive attaches a probability to. But you might reasonably want a probability of frost tonight, or of a 35 C scorcher next week. Those can be worked out from the plain temperature forecast, and then checked the same way.

Read this section differently from the others. The probabilities here were not published by anyone — they were derived from the ordinary temperature and rainfall forecast by learning, from past days, how often each forecast value was followed by the event. So the fact that they come out well calibrated is not a finding: they were built to be. What cannot be faked is resolution and skill — how sharply the forecast separates days when the event happens from days when it does not. That is what the table below shows. Each day was scored by a recipe trained only on other, non-adjacent stretches of time, never on itself.

Skill score by event and days ahead

EventHow often Days ahead
1234567
Hot day (max temp >= 32 C)13%0.840.860.850.820.790.710.66
Extreme heat (max temp >= 35 C)6%0.700.650.680.640.570.470.48
Frost (min temp < 0 C)25%0.700.710.670.640.660.630.56
Rain (>= 0.2 mm)27%0.460.360.330.260.220.150.12

1.00 = perfect, 0.00 = no better than quoting the long-run average for the time of year. Each column is 812 days.

Temperature events stay predictable far longer than rain. Hot day (max temp >= 32 C) is at 0.84 a day ahead and still 0.66 a week out. Rain (>= 0.2 mm) starts lower (0.46) and collapses to 0.12 — close to useless. A week-ahead warning about temperature is worth acting on; a week-ahead rain forecast is barely worth reading.

Because the probability is derived, the recipe could be doing the work rather than the forecast. Two quite different recipes were tried — one assuming a fixed S-shaped curve, one assuming only "more never means less". They disagree by at most 0.063 in skill, so the ranking above is a property of the forecast, not of the method.

Extreme heat is the thinnest result here: only 48 such days occurred in the whole record, so treat its numbers as indicative.

What this does not tell you

  • One lead time only, for the published rain probability. The rain results above cover a short-range forecast, so they do not tell you how far ahead a published probability can be trusted. The frost-and-heat section answers that question for derived probabilities, but those are not what a weather app shows you. A daily logger is accumulating the data for the real thing.
  • We have less evidence than it looks. 731 days sounds like a lot, but weather persists, so the effective sample is about 363 independent days.
  • The gauge is a point, the forecast is a square. The two stations, 10 km apart, disagree about whether it rained on 7.4% of days. No calibration claim finer than that is meaningful. See representativeness.
  • Temperature degrades with lead time, from 1.58 °C average error at 1 day to 2.64 °C at 7 days, with a persistent cold bias at short range.

Glossary

Every technical term used above, in plain language.

PoP — Probability of Precipitation

The number behind "30% chance of rain". It means: across many days that look like this one, it rains on about 30% of them.

It does NOT mean rain over 30% of the city, or for 30% of the day. That misreading is extremely common.
Calibration — also: reliability

Whether those percentages are honest. Take every day the forecast said 30%, and check how often it actually rained. If it is close to 30%, the forecast is calibrated.

A calibration curve just does this for every percentage at once. Points on the diagonal = honest. Below = overpromising rain.
Base rate — climatology

How often it simply rains here, ignoring any forecast.

This is the no-skill baseline. You could say this number every single day and be perfectly calibrated while being useless - which is why calibration alone is not enough.
Brier score — BS

Average squared miss between the promised probability and what happened (1 = it rained, 0 = it did not). Lower is better.

Brier scores are NOT comparable between places. A desert forecaster who always says 2% scores a brilliant Brier score while telling you nothing. That is why the skill score exists.
Brier Skill Score — BSS

How much better than just quoting the long-run average. Higher is better; 1.0 is perfect.

This is the number that actually answers "is the forecast any good?". Operational day-ahead rain forecasts typically land between 0.3 and 0.5.
Reliability term — the honesty penalty

The part of the Brier score caused purely by percentages being dishonest. Zero is perfect.

Compare it to the uncertainty term to judge size. Here it is a few percent of it, which is small.
Resolution term — the discrimination reward

How much the forecast actually separates rainy days from dry ones. Higher is better, capped by the uncertainty term.

This is what proves the forecast is not just hedging toward the base rate every day. Calibration without resolution is useless.
Uncertainty term — difficulty of the problem

How hard forecasting rain is here at all, fixed by the local climate. Not a measure of forecast quality.

It peaks at 0.25 for a 50/50 event. A place where it always or never rains is trivially easy and scores near zero.
ECE — Expected Calibration Error

The average gap between what was promised and what happened, in percentage points. The most directly readable calibration number.

Under 5 points is excellent, 5-10 is good, above 15 is poor.
Sharpness

Willingness to commit to confident numbers like 5% or 95%, instead of mumbling "40%" every day.

Not accuracy - it is the companion to calibration. A useful forecast needs both: honest AND decisive.
Consistency range — perfect-forecast range

How far off the diagonal a point would land even if the forecast were flawless, purely because we only have a limited number of days.

This is what separates real miscalibration from noise. A point inside this range is NOT evidence of a problem, however far from the diagonal it looks.
Effective sample size

How many genuinely independent days we have, which is fewer than the calendar days we collected.

Weather persists: if it rained today it probably rained yesterday. Consecutive days are not independent evidence, so all error bars must use this smaller number.
Block bootstrap

The method used for the error bars. It resamples the data in multi-day chunks rather than single days.

Resampling single days would assume they are independent and produce error bars that are far too narrow.
Isotonic recalibration

Learning a correction that maps the stated percentage onto the one actually observed.

It must be tested on days it was not trained on. Fitted and scored on the same days, it always looks like it helps.
Lead time

How many days ahead the forecast was made. A 3-day lead means predicted three days before the day in question.

Accuracy degrades with lead time; that degradation is usually more useful to know than any single accuracy number.
MAE / bias — Mean Absolute Error

MAE is the average size of the temperature error, ignoring direction. Bias is the average signed error.

They answer different questions. A forecast can have zero bias and still be wildly wrong daily, if errors cancel out.
Representativeness

The forecast covers a grid square of several kilometres; the rain gauge is a single point.

A summer shower can soak the gauge and miss the rest of the square, or vice versa. This looks like forecast error but is not.
ERA5 / reanalysis

A best-estimate reconstruction of past weather, blending a model with observations.

Used only as a cross-check here. Scoring a forecast against a reanalysis from the same centre flatters the forecast, so real station measurements are the primary truth.
Present weather — WMO code table 4677

A code an observer files for what the sky is doing right now: clear, mist, fog, drizzle, rain, snow, thunderstorm.

Used as the hourly truth, because Bucharest stations do not report hourly rain amounts at all. It records whether precipitation is falling, not how much - which actually matches what a probability of precipitation claims.
Observing practice

How often, and by what method, a station files its reports.

A station reporting three times an hour catches more brief showers than one reporting once, so it records more rain for identical weather. That is a property of the observer, not the climate, and it limits how precisely two stations can be compared.
